about.heading: About Me (&) My Journey
about.intro: I wanted to know why some sites pull traffic for free while others pay for every click and still can't be found. Thirty-odd websites later I'm still opening every project with that question.

cards.heading: Marketing, from the ground up
cards.short: BBA Marketing at IMSciences, Peshawar. Four years on consumer behaviour, brand strategy, and why people buy.
cards.long: Four years of BBA Marketing at the Institute of Management Sciences in Peshawar. Consumer behaviour, brand strategy, market research. It sounds far from crawl budgets, but it's the reason I think about the buyer before the channel, and that has been worth more than any tool I've picked up since.

cards.heading: What makes people trust a website
cards.short: Research on trust in e-commerce, and how much perceived risk quietly decides what people will buy.
cards.long: My research looked at consumer trust in e-commerce, using the PROCESS macro and a Sobel test to pull perceived risk out as a mediating variable. Dry stuff on paper. But it's why I don't take a conversion rate at face value now. The number tells you people left. It never tells you what they were worried about.

cards.heading: First audits, first surprises
cards.short: Everyone assumes it's the content. It's usually a redirect chain from a migration nobody has touched since.
cards.long: The first proper audits taught me something I still see nearly every month. Clients are convinced the writing is the problem. It almost never is. It's forty pages sharing one meta title, or a robots rule left behind from staging, or a redirect chain from a migration two years back. Nobody looks, so nothing moves.

cards.heading: The unglamorous half
cards.short: Technical SEO at UnitedSol. Crawl paths, redirect chains, schema, indexation. None of it looks like marketing.
cards.long: UnitedSol is where I went properly deep on the technical side. Crawl budget, indexation gaps, schema, page speed. It's invisible work. No client has ever been excited by a fixed canonical tag. But get it right once and every piece of content you publish afterwards has to work less hard to rank.

cards.heading: Seven sites, seven problems
cards.short: Google Ads and SEO at DX Creativ. Seven live client sites, each broken in its own way.
cards.long: Seven live client sites at DX Creativ, all at once. Technical audits, on-page, content strategy, link building, and Google Ads running alongside. You learn to prioritise fast when there's no chance of fixing everything. Most weeks the job was working out which single change would move the most, then defending why the other twelve could wait.

cards.heading: Paid and organic, same system
cards.short: Performance marketing at Remote Opus. Ads and SEO stopped being two separate jobs.
cards.long: At Remote Opus I run the whole thing. Google and Meta Ads, SEO, landing pages, conversion tracking. Running both sides showed me how much gets wasted keeping them apart. Paid tells you in a fortnight which keywords bring buyers instead of browsers. Organic takes months to work that out on its own.

cards.heading: Still the same question
cards.short: What is actually stopping this site from growing? Everything else follows from the answer.
cards.long: The method hasn't really changed since that first audit. Find what's broken, work out what each thing is costing, fix the expensive ones first, then build around what buyers are already searching for. No templates. And no reporting that quietly buries a bad month.

items.q: How long before I see results?
items.a: Technical fixes can move things in weeks. Content and authority take months. Most projects show something measurable in Search Console somewhere between six and twelve weeks, and the bigger gains come after that. Anyone promising you page one in thirty days is selling something.

items.q: Do you work on paid ads as well as SEO?
items.a: Yes, and I'd rather run both. Paid tells you within a fortnight which keywords bring buyers. Organic takes months to learn the same thing. Keeping them in separate silos throws away the most useful signal you've got.

items.q: What does an SEO audit actually cover?
items.a: A full crawl, then technical, on-page and content review, plus keyword and competitor gap analysis. You get a fix list ordered by impact rather than by effort, and a call where I actually walk you through it instead of emailing a PDF and vanishing.

items.q: Can you work with my existing site?
items.a: That's most of what I do. Technical cleanup, content structure, schema, or a migration handled without dropping rankings. I'd rather step into a build that exists than insist on starting over.

items.q: Which platforms have you worked with?
items.a: WordPress, Shopify, Magento, Strapi and others, across e-commerce, travel, B2B and agency portfolios. The platform changes how easy the fix is. It rarely changes what the fix is.
Yes. Business Profile, local pack visibility, and the service and location pages that turn a nearby search into an enquiry. For service businesses it's often the quickest thing that works.

items.q: How do you report on progress?
items.a: Search Console and analytics, not screenshots of rankings. Impressions, clicks, positions, conversions, what I changed and what it did. If a month goes badly you'll hear it from me before you spot it.

items.q: Not sure what your site needs?
items.a: Send the URL and tell me what's going on. Most audits and strategy calls start within 48 hours, and you'll get an honest read on what's holding the site back. No pitch attached.
